_comment: How a BrickDeal slideshow is dressed: the words on a slide, the words under
the post, and the type that carries them.
Everything here is editorial rather than structural - the set of decisions
that get re-litigated after looking at a week of numbers - so it lives in
one file you can edit without reading any code. src/brick/config.js reads
it, validates it, and is the only module that knows this path.
Read once per process and cached. A malformed file throws at first use
rather than quietly reverting to a default: a post that silently lost its
hashtags looks identical to a post that never had any.
The shape of all of this is copied from @lego_from_ali, the account this
channel is modelled on, with one deliberate departure - see `copy` below.
The trademark rule.
The reference account writes the original brand's name on every slide
('בחנות של לגו: 269₪') and spends one of its five hashtags on it. That tag
is what this audience actually searches, so a blanket ban costs real
discovery.
THE RULE IS NOW ABOUT WHAT THE WORD REFERS TO, not whether it appears.
Naming the brand to say what a price is being compared AGAINST is a
comparison. Naming it to say what is being SOLD is a claim about origin,
and it is not a trademark technicality - it tells somebody they are
getting a thing they are not. So the list label names it (see `labels`)
and nothing else ever does: the products are 'סטים תואמים' on every
surface, on the site, in the captions and in the hashtags.
allowTrademark stays FALSE and should. It is an all-or-nothing switch over
everything a model writes - hooks, titles, captions, tags - and the tag is
the use most likely to draw a complaint, because a tag does not describe a
post, it inserts it into the feed where the brand's own people are looking.
The one place the word belongs is written by hand, in one config value,
and is a comparison.
The three price lines, in this order, on every slide of every deck.
The order and the labels never vary within a deck. A slide whose fields
differ from its neighbour's reads as improvised, and the consistency is
what makes a swipe scan as one post.
`list` is NOT a claim about any Israeli shelf. It is the original brand's
recommended retail price, read off Brickset and converted. See rrp.js.
AND IT NAMES THAT BRAND, which is the one place in this project where the
trademark is written down on purpose. The reasoning, because this is the
kind of line that gets 'corrected' by somebody who only read the guard:
- It said 'מחיר מחירון' for a long time, which was both vaguer and less
honest than the truth. A 'list price' with no issuer named is a number
from nowhere; the number is LEGO's, and saying so is what makes the
comparison mean anything to a viewer.
- Naming a brand to say what you are comparing AGAINST is a different
act from naming it to say what you are SELLING. This line is the
first. The products stay 'סטים תואמים' everywhere, always.
- It is written here by a person, once. The guard in src/brick/copy.js
stays on for everything a model writes - hooks, titles, captions - and
allowTrademark stays false. That switch is all or nothing and would
open the hashtags too, which is the use most likely to draw a
complaint: a tag does not describe a post, it inserts it into the feed
where the brand's own people are looking.
The type on a slide. White, centred, with a fine dark outline and a soft
shadow under it.
THIS IS THE TRAVEL CHANNEL'S TREATMENT, not the reference account's, and
the swap was a deliberate call after looking at both rendered. The
reference sets its type hard against the right edge in a thick black
outline, which is TikTok's own editor style and reads as somebody typing
on a photo in the app. Rendered over our own frames it came out heavier
than the posts this channel already publishes, and the owner picked the
lighter one.
What carries legibility here is therefore NOT the outline - at ~2px it is
an edge rather than a border - it is the scrim and the shadow. That
matters, because a home shot of a white wall in daylight is the one
background where a fine outline struggles and the reference's heavy one
would not. Watch the white-wall column in `npm run brick-lab`; raise
strokePct if it stops holding.
Sizes are fractions of the frame's WIDTH. Three percent of 1080 is 32px;
the same fraction of a 1920-tall frame would be 58px, which is an
eightfold difference in how loud a slide is, so the basis is stated
rather than assumed.
`strokePct` is the outline you can SEE, not the CSS stroke width. The CSS
property is centred on the glyph and half of it is painted over by the
fill, so brickSlide.js doubles this before it writes the rule.
`weight` IS CONSTRAINED BY THE BUNDLED FILE and is not a free dial. The
Hebrew is set in Arimo, and the Arimo in assets/fonts is a single static
SemiBold — 600, no variable axis. 600 is therefore the heaviest Hebrew
these slides can actually draw; 700 here, which is what it said while the
type was Rubik, would be served by Chromium's synthetic bold, and a
smeared outline on an algorithmically fattened glyph is worse than the
real 600. Raising this means bundling a heavier Arimo, not editing the
number.
The hook on the first slide, which is the only thing most viewers read.
First person, conversational, slightly confrontational, hobbyist to
hobbyist. Questions and challenges - never 'SALE', never a percentage.
These are the reference's own covers with the trademark taken out, and
they are handed to the model as the standard a generated hook is measured
against, the same way the travel pipeline carried one real published post.
Also the fallback: a hook the model could not produce, or produced and
failed the copy guard, falls back to one of these rather than to nothing.
*STARS MARK THE EMPHASIS* - the one phrase set in cream instead of white.
Hebrew has no capitals, so the shout a cover needs has to be carried by
colour. It is one phrase and not the whole line on purpose: if every word
is cream then no word is shouted. The stars never reach a slide; config.js
strips them and hands the renderer the phrase separately.
lines: כמה *באמת* צריך לשלם על סט כזה?
זה אותו דגם. *זה לא אותו מחיר.*
_priceComment: The covers that LEAD WITH THE NUMBER instead of asking for a guess.
The account's whole argument is that the same model costs a fraction of
what the original does, and a cover that asks somebody to guess makes
them swipe before they hear it. That is a good trade on a viewer who
already knows this feed and a bad one on a viewer who does not: they
have to spend a swipe to find out whether the post was worth a swipe.
These put the argument on screen in the first second.
`priceLedShare` is how often. Not every post, on purpose - a feed of
price tags reads as a shop, and the guess is the shape that gets the
swipe. Roughly two posts in five lead with the number.
{ours} AND {list} ARE FILLED IN FROM THE FIRST SLIDE'S OWN NUMBERS, the
same two the slide under it prints. Nothing here is written by a model:
the one failure that would matter is a cover quoting a price the post
does not charge, and that is precisely the failure a model cannot be
relied on not to produce. See `priceHook` in src/brick/build.js.
A post only leads with the number when there IS one - the set has a
list price and it is at least two and a half times what we charge.
Below that the gap is not worth shouting and the deck asks for a guess
instead. Set this to [] to turn price-led covers off entirely.
NO BRAND NAME IN ANY OF THEM. 'במקום 400 ₪ בלגו' is the obvious way to
write this line and it is the one thing copy.js refuses outright - the
build throws rather than publishing it. 'במחירון' says the same thing
about the same number and is the word the slides already use.
Stars mark the emphasis, exactly as above. Put them on OUR price: it is
the number the post is about and the one a viewer has to believe.
_swipeComment: The line under the hook that asks for the swipe.
A cover asks a question and then has to give somebody something to DO
with it. Without this the first slide is a rhetorical question on a
photograph, and the swipe rate is whatever curiosity alone buys.
Quieter and smaller than the hook on purpose. It is an instruction, not
the argument - if it competes with the question for attention it has
taken the attention the question needed.
The arrow points LEFT because these slides are Hebrew: in a right to
left post the next thing is to the left. Set it to an empty string to
turn the line off entirely.
IT NAMES THE BRAND, and this is the second and last place that happens -
the other is `labels.list`. Both are the same kind of use and neither is
an exception to the rule in `copy`: the word says what the price is being
measured AGAINST, never what is being sold.
It is here rather than in the hook for a reason that is about machinery
rather than taste. The hook is written by a model and the guard is
binary, so allowing the word there would also allow 'לגו בשליש מהמחיר',
which reads as though we sell it. This line is written by hand, once,
and cannot drift. It also does the comprehension work the hook could not
do in six words: a viewer who has never heard of 'סטים תואמים' now knows
in one glance what is being compared, and has a reason to swipe.
`swipePriceHe` IS THE SAME LINE FOR A COVER THAT LED WITH THE NUMBER.
The ordinary one offers to show what the set costs at the original
brand, and a price-led cover has just printed that number - offering to
reveal it underneath is the post arguing with its own first slide. So
that cover offers the only thing it has not shown yet: the rest of the
sets. Leave it empty and price-led covers use the ordinary line.

_comment: One or two sentences, then the call to the community, then a separator,
then the tags. The reference's exact shape.
`cta` carries NO URL and that is enforced, not trusted: format.js refuses
a caption containing one. An external domain in a TikTok description is a
demotion and the string was never tappable on either platform anyway - the
community is reachable from the bio, which is where the link lives.

_engageComment: The ask for a comment, drawn fresh per post and set on its own line
above the link.
`cta` was the only call to action and it points OFF the post - to the
community, in another app. That is the conversion, and it is worth
having, but it does nothing for the post itself: a viewer who taps it
has left. A comment is the opposite. It costs the viewer a second, it
happens without leaving, and it is the signal these platforms actually
rank on.
TWO QUESTIONS, ASKED IN VARIATIONS. 'איזה סט הבא?' and 'הייתם קונים?'
are the pool, and everything in it is one of the two.
They are the two an ordinary viewer can answer without thinking, which
is the whole requirement - an ask that needs a considered reply gets a
considered silence. The first hands the viewer the next post's subject
and every answer is a set name, so the replies double as the request
queue. The second is a yes or a no about a price they have just been
shown, and either answer is an opinion about the number, which is the
post's own argument coming back in somebody else's words.
The pair about guessing the price is kept because it CLOSES A LOOP THE
COVER OPENS: the cover asks what the set cost, the caption asks them to
say the number out loud, and somebody who has already guessed silently
is most of the way to typing it.
WHAT WAS TAKEN OUT: the tag-a-friend line and the save-the-post line.
Both are fine asks and neither is a comment - they buy a share and a
bookmark, and this line's one job is to get a reply in the thread.
Nothing here promises a reply, a DM or a link in exchange for a
comment. That is engagement bait, the platforms demote it, and we
could not honour it anyway - there is nothing on the other end.
engage: איזה סט לבדוק בפוסט הבא? תגיבו 👇
הייתם קונים את זה במחיר הזה? תגיבו 💬

_followComment: The reason to follow. Last line of the description, under the link and
Every other line in the caption is about THIS post. This one is the only
line about the next one, which is why it closes: a reader who has got
this far is finished with the post in front of them, and that is the
only moment an argument for another one is worth anything.
IT IS A REASON, NOT AN INSTRUCTION. 'עוקבים?' on its own asks for a
follow and offers nothing back for it; every line here says what the
next post actually contains - more sets, checked, with the prices. That
is the only honest case for following a feed, and it is a case this
account can make, because the next post genuinely is that.
NOTHING HERE CARRIES AN EMOJI, and that is the one visible difference
from the pools above. The hook has one, the comment ask has one and the
cta has its pin - three, which is the whole budget this file sets. A
fourth would spend it, and of the four lines this is the one that reads
best flat: a plain sentence about what is coming next is a promise, the
same sentence with a bell after it is an advert for a promise.
Set to an empty array to turn the line off. The caption then has the
shape it had before this existed, which is still a valid one.

_comment: The last slide, and the only branded frame in the post.
It exists because the watermark does not. A line of type across the
bottom of every slide is the clearest tell that a post is an ad; one
closing frame asks once, at the moment somebody has already watched the
whole thing, which is the only moment the ask is worth anything.
THE CAPTION MAY NOT CARRY A URL - assertNoUrl refuses one at build time,
because a link in a caption is what the platforms demote. A SLIDE is not
a caption and no such rule applies to it: the domain here is pixels in a
photograph, which nothing can parse, follow or rank.
Four lines and no more. The ask, where to go, why to follow, and the
address.
`followHe` IS THE ONLY ASK ON THIS FRAME THAT COSTS THE VIEWER NOTHING
AND DOES NOT MOVE THEM. `whereHe` sends them to another app and the
address sends them to a browser; both are worth having and both end the
session. A follow happens in place, in one tap, and it is the only thing
here that makes the next post reach the person who watched this one.
One fixed line rather than a pool, unlike the caption's. Every post
closes on this same frame and that repetition is the point - it is the
one thing in the post a returning viewer recognises - so the sentence on
it settles instead of varying. Set it to an empty string to drop the
line; the frame then has the three it had before.
It says what following gets you, not that you should. 'עקבו' alone is an
instruction on a slide nobody asked for; this names the next post.
endCard.followHe: עקבו לעוד סטים ומחירים כל שבוע

_comment: Exactly broadCount + nicheCount tags under every post - five, by default.
Broad tags buy the first impressions and niche tags decide who the post is
then shown to, so the split matters more than the total. The reference
mixes English reach tags with Hebrew niche ones and that is copied here.
`useTheme` spends ONE of the niche slots on a tag generated from the
deck's own theme - #הארי_פוטר on a Harry Potter deck - rather than adding
a sixth. The count stays five either way; a deck whose theme did not
resolve falls back to the niche pool.
Note what is NOT here. #לגו is the tag this audience searches and the
reference spends a slot on it. See `copy` above.
How many sets go in one post, and how cheap a set has to be to anchor a
price roundup.
Five is the reference's count and it is not arbitrary: five slides is five
chances to hook a viewer in one post, and each swipe is a watch-time
signal. Below three the post reads as thin; above seven the last slides
are seen by almost nobody.
